analysis.one_liner: Creates a water and sewer infrastructure trust fund paid for by raising the corporate tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its March 2023 referral, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no further action for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a dedicated federal trust fund — capped at $35 billion a year, or a share of EPA's 20-year water-need estimates — to pay for clean water and drinking water projects. The money would come from raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%. It would fund lead pipe replacement grants, water system upgrades for PFAS ('forever chemical') contamination, lead-free drinking water in schools, rural household wells, tribal water facilities, and border-colonias water systems. It would also steer state revolving loan funds toward publicly owned water systems, allow those funds to buy private water companies, require half the funds go to grants rather than loans, and require study of water affordability and discrimination in water service.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing unaffordable water bills or shutoffs, people served by water systems with lead pipes or PFAS contamination, schoolchildren drinking from lead-laden fountains, rural families on private wells, tribal communities, and border colonias. Water and sewer construction workers also gain, since the bill preserves prevailing-wage rules and encourages project labor agreements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with lead, PFAS, or unaffordable water

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a Water Affordability, Transparency, Equity, and Reliability Trust Fund, capped at $35 billion a year or one-twentieth of EPA's combined 20-year clean water and drinking water need estimates, and spends it through defined grant allocations [S3].

Funds lead service line replacement grants for property owners, treatment plant and water-source upgrades where systems are contaminated with PFAS, and filtration grants for contaminated household wells [S3].
Expands the school drinking water program from $5 million to $1.05 billion a year to install lead-free fountains, coolers, and bottle-filling stations and to monitor lead in school water [S3].

Requires state drinking water funds to prioritize publicly owned, operated, and managed water systems and permits use of those funds to purchase privately owned water systems, with an exception for small systems serving under 10,000 people [S3].

Requires at least 50% of state revolving fund money to go to additional subsidization (grants or loan forgiveness rather than loans), and bars states from using clean water funds for projects that mainly benefit new suburban subdivisions [S3].

Directs EPA to study and report on water rates, shutoffs for unpaid bills, tax liens and foreclosures tied to water debt, discriminatory practices by providers and state funding administrators, and public participation in water system regionalization [S3].
Preserves prevailing wage requirements on funded projects and requires states to permit and, to the maximum extent practicable, use project labor agreements for construction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations bear the funding cost directly: the corporate income tax rate rises from 21% to 24.5% on taxable years after December 31, 2022, with the added revenue dedicated to the fund. Shareholders and, to the extent taxes are passed through, business customers ultimately absorb some of that cost. Land developers of new communities lose access to subsidized water infrastructure for new subdivisions.

drawbacks.text: The bill is funded by a 3.5-point corporate tax increase of up to $35 billion a year, which some economists argue is partly borne by workers and consumers through lower wages and higher prices, and which would have faced firm opposition from business groups [S3].

State revolving funds could be used to purchase privately owned water systems from a 'willing or unwilling seller,' which raises contentious questions about forcing private owners to sell public infrastructure [S3].
Requiring project labor agreements on most funded construction can raise project costs and limits participation by non-union contractors [S3].
Barring revolving-fund assistance for projects that substantially benefit new communities, except decentralized wastewater systems, could slow water infrastructure for growing areas [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and specific: lead and PFAS exposure, unaffordable water bills, and shutoffs for water debt are documented problems, and dedicated grant funding plus a requirement that half the money be grants rather than loans directly addresses them. The main costs are real but diffuse — a 3.5-point corporate tax increase shared across businesses and consumers, and rules (public-ownership preference, project labor agreements, the new-community ban) that some utilities, developers, and contractors would contest. On balance the bill's costs fall on broad corporate taxpayers while its benefits reach households with direct health and affordability harms, though its strong provisions for organized labor and against privatization would have made it harder to pass than a simpler infrastructure bill.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in March 2023 and sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, it never got a committee vote or a floor vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Water Affordability, Transparency, Equity, and Reliability Act on March 22, 2023, joined by five Democratic senators — Wyden, Blumenthal, Merkley, Warren, and Welch [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; that was the bill's last recorded action [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a markup or vote on the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, corporations keep the 21% corporate tax rate rather than funding a water trust fund, and private water companies face no federal push toward sale or public ownership.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded, but all six original supporters were Democratic-caucus senators and no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committee without either party being forced to take a position on the record.

industries.note: The bill raises the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5% to fund up to $35 billion a year in water infrastructure. That is the direct cost of the program, and keeping the current rate is what corporate interests got when the bill died in committee.

The bill requires state drinking water funds to prioritize publicly owned systems and lets those funds purchase privately owned water systems from a willing or unwilling seller. Private water companies profit by charging ratepayers, so the bill's push toward public ownership runs against their business model.

The bill would direct tens of billions of dollars a year into water and sewer construction, but it requires project labor agreements on most funded projects, which limits participation by non-union contractors and can raise bid costs.

industries.industry: Land developers of new residential communities
industries.note: States would be barred from using clean water revolving funds for projects that substantially benefit new communities, lots, or subdivisions, except advanced decentralized wastewater systems, so subsidized water infrastructure for new sprawl would end.

industries.industry: Public water systems and municipal utilities
industries.note: The bill channels dedicated funding to publicly owned systems for lead pipe replacement, PFAS treatment, and upgrades, with at least half the state revolving fund money required to go to grants or loan forgiveness rather than loans.
